issues.title: Your RAG answer is wrong: retrieval or the model?
issues.dek: A three-minute test that tells you which half of a retrieval system failed, before anyone changes a prompt or swaps a model.

body.text: A team ships a documentation assistant. In week one it answers a question about the refund window with a figure nobody recognises. The fix that gets tried first is almost always the same: a stronger model, then a longer prompt, then a plea to the vendor. Weeks go by. The answer stays wrong.

The uncomfortable part is that none of those steps were diagnostic. They were guesses about which half of the system failed, made without looking. And a retrieval system only has two halves worth separating: what got fetched, and what the model did with it.
Look at the retrieved text before you touch the prompt.

items: Take the failing question and log the exact chunks that were retrieved for it, in the order they were passed.
Read them yourself. Does the correct answer appear anywhere in that text, in plain words?
If it does not appear, the retrieval half failed and no prompt will fix it.

If it does appear, paste the same chunks into a fresh chat with the same question. If the model now answers correctly, your assembly is at fault: order, truncation or a conflicting instruction. If it still answers wrongly, the model half failed.
Write down which half it was, next to the question, and keep the note. Five of those notes is a pattern.

body.text: Most teams who run this honestly for a week find the split lands somewhere near two thirds retrieval, one third everything else. That is not a law of nature, but it is common enough to be worth expecting: the model is usually doing a reasonable job on text that never should have been handed to it.
What each half actually breaks on

rows: The right passage was never fetched
Chunk size, the index's freshness, and whether the query is embedded the same way as the documents
The right passage was fetched and then cut off
Token budget and truncation order: the useful chunk is often last
The passage is present but contradicted
A system prompt, an older summary, or a memory note that disagrees with it
The passage is present, clear, and ignored
Instruction conflict, or asking for a format the content cannot fill
The passage is absent and an answer appears anyway
No instruction to decline, and no check that the claim is grounded

body.text: Once you know which half fails, the engineering choice is no longer a matter of taste. A retrieval failure is a data and indexing problem: reindex on a schedule, chunk on headings rather than character counts, and store the document date so stale text can be filtered out instead of out-argued. A model failure is a design problem: supply the fact rather than ask for it, require a quotation from the source, and allow the answer “not in the documents” to be a success rather than a defect.

There is also a third outcome worth naming. Sometimes the retrieved text is correct, the model's answer is correct, and the user still calls it wrong — because the document itself is out of date. That is not an AI failure at all. It is a content problem that the assistant has made visible, and the honest response is to fix the document.

items: Pick the three complaints you have heard most about your assistant and run the three-minute test on each.
Log the retrieved chunks for every answer from now on. A system you cannot inspect is a system you can only guess about.
Add one test to your evaluation set per confirmed failure, with the question and the answer you expect, so the next change has to keep passing it.

body.text: The point is not the test itself. It is the habit of naming the failing part before changing anything — the same habit the ExplAIn course builds across all eight parts of an AI system, starting with the map in Module 00.

issues.takeaway: Read the retrieved text before you blame the model: if the answer was never fetched, no prompt can save it.
